sweep_summary: Ten title hits for Maltese (all Glottolog). Read this search of works with stress in the title: Grice, Vella & Bruggeman 2019 (J. Phonetics, open OAR@UM copy, held by the project) gives Vella's own first-hand rule on p.2 sec. 2.1 — rightmost heavy syllable (V:/VC), closed final only if superheavy, default penult, stress final/penult/antepenult — confirming and refining the catalog's weight coding and superseding the second-hand Galea 2016 restatement as deciding source. Newly downloaded and read: Vella 2003 ICPhS (phrase accents/intonation; silent on stress placement) and Grech & Vella 2015 ICPhS (Maltese English rhythm; other variety). Not obtainable today: Puech 2011 'Syllabic structure and stress in Maltese' (De Gruyter, paywalled, priority high — dedicated treatment independent of the Vella lineage), Vella 1995 Edinburgh PhD (ERA unreachable; priority high as the primary source), Vella 2009 'On Maltese prosody' (Benjamins, paywalled, priority medium; two Glottolog records, one with editor Comrie miscarried as co-author). Calleja 1987 and Debrincat 1999 are University of Malta undergraduate dissertations on Maltese English (per Grech & Vella 2015 refs 9 and 11), not relevant. Discovery channels (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Google Books API, scholar.archive.org, BASE, CORE, OAR@UM) were all exhausted or bot-could not be reached by automated download on 2026-09-17.

new_statements.quote: In Maltese, lexical stress is assigned on phonological grounds to the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. It falls on the heavy (V: or VC) syllable closest to the right edge of the word, except in words having a closed final syllable, which can only be stressed if it is superheavy (V:C or VCC). In words in which there is no heavy syllable, lexical stress is penultimate by default (Vella, 2009).
new_statements.citation: Grice, Martine, Alexandra Vella & Anna Bruggeman (2019). Stress, pitch accent, and beyond: Intonation in Maltese questions. Journal of Phonetics 76: 100913. doi:10.1016/j.wocn.2019.100913 (open copy OAR@UM handle 123456789/74793).
new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive stress at the right edge: the rightmost heavy syllable (long vowel or closed syllable) is stressed, a closed word-final syllable counts as heavy only if superheavy (V:C or VCC, i.e. final consonant extrametrical), and with no heavy syllable stress defaults to the penult; stress may therefore be final, penultimate or antepenultimate. This matches the catalog's 'weight' coding field for field and adds that antepenultimate stress occurs (a point the catalog's Sutcliffe-derived 'never earlier than penult' line hedges).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Grice, Vella & Bruggeman 2019 statement (final if superheavy, otherwise heavy penult, otherwise further left; antepenultimate stress exists; plain closed final syllables are not stressed) and consistent with the catalog's weight coding. It adds the classical three-clause formulation, the heavy/superheavy distinction for finals, monosyllable and final-long-vowel cases, the loanword adaptation to penult, and the cyclic secondary-stress question. One formulation-level difference: Wolf's clause (1c) assigns antepenult stress whenever the penult is light (including pre-syncope L.L.L strings), whereas the Grice/Vella 2009 statement defaults to the penult when no hea…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Right-edge weight-sensitive stress in the Brame (1972, 1974) formulation: stress the final syllable if it is superheavy (CVCC or CVːC; monosyllables are also stressed), otherwise the penult if it is heavy (CVC or CVː, or the word is disyllabic), otherwise the antepenult. A plain closed final syllable (CVC) does not attract stress; only superheavy finals do (p.8). Wolf calls the non-final part 'of the Latin type: stress the penult if heavy, else stress the antepenult' (p.8) and models it as a right-aligned moraic trochee with the final syllable unfootable. He notes that clause (1c) is disputed by Puech (2011), who has syncope precede stress so that surface forms like [ˈʔat.lu] simply get penult stress, and endnote 4 remarks that in parallel OT the antepenult case can be read as a surface preference for penult stress on heavy syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.3: the cyclic analysis posits a secondary stress on the initial syllable of object-suffixed forms such as [ˌħa.ˈtaf.na] 'he snatched us', but 'the secondary stresses.. are not reported in descriptions of Maltese (e.g. Aquilina 1959: 68); Brame (1974: 44) acknowledges this, suggesting that, if needs be, the secondary stress may be deleted by a late rule ordered after syncope.' So secondary stress is a theoretical construct here, not a reported surface fact.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllables are stressed on their sole (final) syllable (p.8). Final stress on a few native words ending in a diphthong, e.g. Mulej [mʊ.ˈlɛɪ] 'Lord' (Vella 2009: 66-68), and on word-final long vowels in loans, chiefly Italian, written with a grave accent (p.8-9, ex. 21). Loans with antepenult stress are adapted to penult, e.g. English ˈArabic → Maltese e.ˈre.bic, Aˈmerica → aˈmeːrka (p.2, endnote 5). Endnote 14: Borg (1997: 251-252) reports stressed [VC#] derived from underlying [VCC#]. Endnote 2: the system 'closely resembles those of the Levantine Arabic dialects'. Stress is assigned cyclically before object suffixes in C-final verb stems (syncope underapplies), but not in vowel-final (third-weak-radical) stems, the paper's main topic.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened entries are one work (Wolf's lingBuzz/001319 paper, later the 2016 Equinox chapter) describing Standard Maltese, using data from Sutcliffe 1936, Aquilina 1959/1965, Borg 1997, Odden 1990/1993 and Vella 2003/2009; no regional dialect is specified. Wolf's endnote 2 places the system alongside Levantine Arabic dialects. Vella 1995 (not opened) concerns Maltese and its influence on Maltese English.

new_statements.quote: Thus, with the exception of some of the more recent loans into the language which have not yet fully assimilated to the phonological system of Maltese, I assume lexical stress in Maltese to operate according to the following rule: Lexical Stress Stress falls on the syllable which is [+heavy]. In words containing no [+heavy] syllable, stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Furthermore, I assume a heavy syllable in Maltese to consist either of a long vowel or diphthong followed optionally by a consonant, or of a short vowel followed either by any permissible syllable coda or by a geminate. (p. 64a) [also p. 56: 'the accounts agree that lexical stress in Maltese is generally either final or penultimate.']

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule; the existing statement (Grice, Vella & Bruggeman 2019) codes Maltese as weight-sensitive at the right edge with penult default and possible antepenultimate stress. Vella 1995 gives the same type and the same outcomes (final/penultimate, antepenultimate when only the antepenult is heavy, penult default) and adds the heavy-syllable definition (geminates count), the one-heavy-syllable-per-word claim, the loanword exception class, and the morphological stress-shift data. One difference in formulation, not in placement type: the 1995 rule does not state the 2019 paper's condition that a closed word-final syllable attracts stress only if…
new_statements.rule_in_words: weight-sensitive word stress: stress goes to the heavy syllable (long vowel or diphthong, optionally closed; or short vowel closed by a permissible coda or a geminate); a word with no heavy syllable takes penultimate stress by default. Vella argues (p. 64b) that an unstressed syllable becomes light so a word has at most one heavy syllable, making Borg's 'nearest the final boundary' clause unnecessary; morphology that makes a later syllable heavy shifts stress to it ('Malti ~ Mal'tin, 'bierek ~ be'rikt, 'qtilna ~ qtil'niehom). Outcome: stress is generally final or penultimate (p. 56, p. 79), antepenultimate when the antepenult is heavy and penult and final are light (p. 63), which she argues is a native pattern, not merely a 'foreign stress-pattern' (p. 59). The section also reviews Sutcliffe 1936 (final if last syllable has a long vowel or V+CC, else penultimate; never earlier than the penult except unassimilated loans), Aquilina 1959/1965 (one main stress, penultimate or final; 'all long vowels are stressed'), Brame 1972a/1974 (V -> [+str] / __ C0((VC)VC0^1)] plus syncope) and A. Borg 1973/1975 (stress on the long nucleus nearest the final boundary, else on the short vowel before the last cluster, else penultimate).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress within Maltese words in sec. 2.2.2 (Aquilina 1965:30 is quoted: 'In the same word there can be one main primary stress, either on the penultimate or the last syllable'). Secondary stress is discussed only for Maltese English compounds/phrases (sec. 2.3.2.2) and at the I-phrase level (ch. 4), not as a Maltese word-level rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Recent loans 'which have not yet fully assimilated to the phonological system of Maltese' are exempted from the rule (p. 64a); antepenultimate stress in loans of Italian/English origin (a'nalizi, 'ciniku, ka'tastrofi, 'terminus) with an ongoing tendency to regularise to penultimate by syncope (ar'tiklu, 'stupdu, 'muzka, 'Napli, 'Tripli) blocked where the resulting cluster is phonotactically bad ('Korsika, not *'Korska) (pp. 57-59); negative suffix -x draws stress to the final syllable with vowel lengthening (ma jis'tax), per Sutcliffe's remark, which Vella reads as an underlying -VC suffix (p. 60).
new_statements.identity_note: Standard Maltese as described by a native-speaker linguist (University of Malta data); the thesis also treats Maltese English (sec. 2.3, ch. 5), whose stress remarks (SE antepenultimate/pre-antepenultimate stress shifting rightward in ME) are about that English variety, not Maltese, and were not used for the reading.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: Wolf (2012/2016) and the existing Grice, Vella & Bruggeman 2019 statement both give right-edge weight-sensitive stress in which a superheavy (CVCC/CVːC) final is stressed, a plain CVC final is not, a heavy penult is stressed, and stress can fall on the antepenult. The formulations differ in the default clause: Wolf's Brame-style rule (1c) says 'else on the antepenult' (so a pre-syncope L.L.L string is stressed on the antepenult), while Grice et al. (after Vella 2009) default to the penult when there is no heavy syllable; Wolf notes on p.2 that clause (1c) is contested (Puech 2011 has syncope feed penult stress, e.g. [ˈʔat.lu]) and that loans with antepenult stress are nativised with penult stress (e.ˈre.bic, aˈmeːrka), so at the surface the two agree. Wolf's rule (1) would also assign antepenult stress to H.L.L words (light penult); the earlier search's census file in this directory (Galea 2016 forms) found the ten H.L.L forms penult-stressed, which bears on that clause but was not re-examined here. Secondary stress: Wolf's cyclic analysis posits it, but he states it is not reported in descriptions of Maltese. Vella 1995 could not be opened (era.ed.ac.uk unreachable, two attempts).

sources.quote: In Maltese, lexical stress is assigned on phonological grounds to the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable. It falls on the heavy (V: or VC) syllable closest to the right edge of the word, except in words having a closed final syllable, which can only be stressed if it is superheavy (V:C or VCC). In words in which there is no heavy syllable, lexical stress is penultimate by default (Vella, 2009).
sources.note: First-hand (Vella is co-author) statement of the Maltese word-stress rule: weight-sensitive, rightmost heavy syllable (V: or VC heavy), a closed final syllable counts only if superheavy (V:C/VCC), default penultimate when no heavy syllable; stress can be final, penult or antepenult. The rest of the paper is about intonation (pitch accents/phrase accents in question-word interrogatives).

sources.note: Intonational phonology only: phrase accents (L-, H-) and boundary tones after the nuclear pitch accent; presupposes lexical stress (phrase accents dock on 'the stressed syllable closest to the edge of the I-phrase') but says nothing about where word stress falls.
